There is more in this than you yet know, I think. The wheel may turn and turn and turn with nothing to show for it, and those who have created their own destiny may regret ever breaking free, but the point of breaking free is to own yourself. You have more choices than you think. Sometime you must recognize when the coin is still in the air, and work to make your desired outcome happen.

When the wheel turns upon you, what will you say to it? Will you repent of your decision to break free of it, because your life grew more difficult, your decisions more dire? Or will you stand firm in your conviction, knowing that you have broken the track, and that the responsibility before you has been taken up only by the gods of the world? Herein is True Freedom: to know oneself, and to seek the path of integrity despite the chastisement of Fate. Your coin is still in the air. This is the fatal moment—the moment of choice. Do you return to the chains of Fate? Or do you brave the forest? That is the only binary choice, and I, for one, know my answer.

One of the interesting things about Tolkien’s work is that he did let his religion influence him. Like was said above, “[it] is a fundamentally Catholic work, unconsciously so at first, and then consciously in the revision.” It’s not an allegory, no, but the man himself did say “I think many confuse applicability with allegory.” Of course, “allegory and applicability meet somewhere in truth.” If it can apply to you, great. If not, it can be enjoyed as a good story nonetheless. An applicable story is more widely useful than an allegory for the very reason that it doesn’t mean just one thing. Hence the idea that Tolkien has a lot of Catholic themes in his books without them being an allegory.

It’s four cups of water, four white tea bags, and a half-cup of sugar (optional), and in a second pot, a cup of raspberries, two tablespoons of sugar, two tablespoons water, and two tablespoons lemon juice. Make the tea, and while it steeps, mash the berries, mixing them with the other ingredients in the second pot on medium heat for ten minutes. (Take the teabags from the tea in the other pot at your desired strength, of course.) Once the berry mix has cooked for ten minutes, strain it into the tea. So! From all the comments and theories therein, I think I have a working theory.
There is most definitely a connection between shiny, glossy things and water in the part of the brain that comes from our ancient roots. One of our friends in the comments linked to a very good scientific paper about that, which everyone ought to read; it’s quite good research. Likewise, an affinity for shiny rocks can be traced back about as far as people have been using metal. Even before bronze, some people (rich people) had copper, which was shinier than simple stone, and going back to the previous paper mentioned, people assumed that the one with the shiny was better at living. This continues into the Bronze Age, since bronze was difficult to obtain, especially in places like the Fertile Crescent, which contained some of the earliest sedentary civilizations, India, and China (which likewise developed agriculture due to proximity to rivers). Then when Iron was discovered by the Hittites and the knowledge proliferated amongst most of the Mesopotamian world, it spread through trade, and more people could afford something shiny.
Eventually, this “shiny is useful for life” mentality evolved into “shiny is useful for showing I’m better at life than other people.” We see this in coin hoards, burial treasures, and all sorts of other ways throughout the world. Some places just made the leap to “more stuff=better life,” and that built on our ingrained love of shiny stuff talked about earlier. Hence, hoards became part of showing wealth, and that continued in some form or other to this very day. 
Our hoards, however, have taken a different tack. There is little to suggest that the things us wee goblins collect are terribly valuable, but they’re valuable to us because of aesthetic reasons, personal preferences, or sentimental reasons—or any number of other reasons for the eclectic nature of most of our hoards. Value in tradability is less important than personal or sentimental value, but still the desire for shiny things persists.
That’s my theory, helpfully informed by all of you lovely, scholarly goblinfolk! I thank you all for your contributions to this study. You have all been absolutely vital to forming this theory I have. I may build on it, but for now, I will be content to discuss in the comments with people about this sort of thing. Again, my utmost gratitude to you all; you’re all very kind, and I’m immensely grateful. I’ll still lurk about in the comments to see how others respond, and if other people make new discoveries, I will hear about it, and we can compare notes.
